Abstract
The Indian Western Himalayan (IWH) region experiences persistent threats from 
natural hazards mainly influenced by land use and land cover (LULC) changes 
resulting from rapid urbanization.

ts from 
natural hazards mainly influenced by land use and land cover (LULC) changes 
resulting from rapid urbanization. The present study aims to perform machine 
learning-based LULC classification for the years 2016, 2019, and 2022 and the 
prediction of future LULC for 2035 using Multi-layer Perceptron Artificial Neural 
Network-Markov Chain model (MLP-ANN-MCM). LULC map was prepared using 
Sentinel-2 imagery in Google Earth Engine (GEE), and eight LULC classes were 
identified with dominance of dense vegetation, scrubland, and barren land. Rapid 
urban growth and declines in natural habitats were observed from the LULC 
transition analysis.

urban growth and declines in natural habitats were observed from the LULC 
transition analysis. The kappa statistics validate the accuracy of the model for 
LULC prediction. Predicted LULC for 2035 indicates an increment in built-up and 
agricultural areas. The study promotes sustainable development and resilience by 
emphasizing effective land use planning.

1.1  Land use land cover change analysis and implications for sustainable development
Sustainable development relies on alterations in land use and land cover (LULC), which 
stand out as critical contributors to global environmental shifts [14]. Understanding the 
status of LULC and its characterization is considered a step toward achieving sustain­
able development.

erstanding the 
status of LULC and its characterization is considered a step toward achieving sustain­
able development. Land use and land cover are related to the socio-economic and natu­
ral attributes of land,therefore, they can be linked to different environmental changes 
[91]. Any shifting in LULC will impact the natural processes that are taking place on 
the earth's surface. Eniolorunda et al. [34], Yang et al. [119], Surya et al. [101], Koroso 
et al. [58], and Arifeen et al. [14] highlight the importance of assessing changes in the 
landscape pattern that occurs during urbanization in urban planning and sustainability.

nce of assessing changes in the 
landscape pattern that occurs during urbanization in urban planning and sustainability. 
With economic growth and the increasing needs of the urban population, the quality 
of the environment is declining due to rising pollution, biodiversity loss, and the deple­
tion of natural resources. Rapid land use conversion occurs due to the pressure rising 
from population migration and urbanization [16]. At present, the development of any 
region does not depend solely on economic growth; it is based on sustainable develop­
ment.

region does not depend solely on economic growth; it is based on sustainable develop­
ment. Sustainable development involves managing the natural environment to support 
economic sustainability and enhance living standards, and it also depends on renewable 
resources to maintain environmental equilibrium [98].
There are 17 Sustainable development Goals (SDGs), including 169 targets proposed 
by the United Nations, directly or indirectly related to LULC [105]. Out of the 17 goals, 
the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals 2, 11, and 13 are directly 
aligned with the land use land cover changes.

Random Forest creates an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a random sub­

is determined through a voting mechanism, where the majority class predicted by the 
individual trees is chosen as the overall prediction [21].

Globally, rapid urbanisation and unregulated urban expansion have driven widespread land use and land cover 
(LULC) changes, resulting in deforestation, loss of vegetation, and depletion of water bodies.

1. Introduction
The patterns of land use and land cover (LULC) have been modified 
by human activities for thousands of years, but in the last century, those 
changes have increased significantly, as the population has grown at a 
fast rate, food needs have risen, and socio-economic development has 
been developed [1,2]. The changes cause severe ecosystem changes, 
which influence hydrological processes, biophysical interactions, and 
environmental stability in complex socio-ecological structures [3,4].

ological processes, biophysical interactions, and 
environmental stability in complex socio-ecological structures [3,4]. 
Conversion of natural landscapes into croplands and urban settlements 
has increased the stressors faced by food security and the sustainability 
of the environment with almost 62% of the land areas being transformed 
[5,6]. Increase in population, growth in urban areas, changes in farming, 
energy demand, deforestation and massive land conversion processes 
are the main causes of LULC change [7,8].

are the main causes of LULC change [7,8]. The insights into these

the interconnected dynamisms of social, environmental, institutional 
and economic forces [9].

2. Materials and methods
The research is an amalgamation of multi-temporal remote sensing 
methods, spatial analysis of GIS, and predictive modelling to evaluate 
the historical LULC evolution between 2001 and 2023 and simulate a 
future land use scenario by 2033.
2.1. Study area
Berhampore is a municipal city in the Murshidabad district of West 
Bengal, India, and serves as the district administrative headquarters 
(Fig. 1). It is the seventh-largest urban agglomeration in the state, 
geographically located between 23◦50′N-24◦10′N latitude and 88◦10′E- 
88◦25′E longitude.

approximately 200 km northeast of Kolkata. The region experiences a 
tropical climate, with temperature extremes ranging from 8.8◦C in 
winter to 42.4◦C during summer.
Administratively, Berhampore comprises 25 municipal wards. The

4. Discussion
This research paper aimed to cope up with one of the major short­
comings of current LULC studies on the rapidly urbanising medium- 
sized Indian cities, that is, the absence of integrated modelling frame­
works which can combine spatially explicit geospatial analysis with 
future urbanisation forecasting models that can reflect both historic land 
transitions and future urbanisation expansion.

ture urbanisation forecasting models that can reflect both historic land 
transitions and future urbanisation expansion. Using an ANN-CA 
modelling framework with support of multi-temporal remote sensing 
and GIS data, the study offers a systematic explanation of the observed 
trends in LULC in Berhampore and assesses the future development of 
the land use.
The findings show that Berhampore has experienced a significant 
change in LULC in the last 20 years, and this has mainly been brought 
about by the high rate of urban growth.

change in LULC in the last 20 years, and this has mainly been brought 
about by the high rate of urban growth. The area of built-up land has 
increased more than twice in the period between 2001 and 2023, and 
the natural vegetation has significantly reduced, as well as water bodies 
have decreased, due to the land conversion processes that are driven by 
urbanisation [66]. These trends are in line with the wider trends of ur­
banisation that have been recorded in various Indian cities with un­
controlled or semi-controlled development.
The use of vegetated and open land into impervious surfaces has 
significant effects on the environment.

potential modelling and Cellular Automata simulation was found to be 
useful not only in obtaining the non-linear relationships between spatial

4.1. Implications, limitations, and future research directions
This study has demonstrated the relevance of the predictive LULC 
modelling to the city planning process to predict the future land use 
pressures. However, certain limitations must be acknowledged. The 
analysis is based on the historical satellite monitoring 2001-2023 and 
excludes the real-time monitoring potentials.

the data.
Future studies ought to incorporate socio-economic changes, cli­
matic conditions and high-frequency satellites to come up with more 
comprehensive and dynamic models of urban growth. The data rele­
vance and applicability of predictive LULC frameworks can also be

5. Conclusion and recommendations
This paper recorded significant LULC changes in Berhampore, West 
Bengal, over 2001 -2023 and showed that an ANN-CA modelling 
structure could be used to simulate future urban development. The 
findings indicate that the built-up areas are increasing rapidly at the 
expense of vegetation cover and the water bodies with a resultant strain 
on the natural landscapes.

indication of further urbanisation, farming land as a ruling class, and 
low forest cover, which points to the possible environmental stresses in 
the long-term, as long as the present-day land use rates persist. The 
associated spatial patterns highlight the role of the (infrastructure) vi­
cinity and population density on urban development processes. The 
combination of multi-temporal data with remote sensing, GIS-based

Abstract
Accurate land use/land cover (LULC) mapping in the Himalayan region remains 
challenging because of its rugged terrain, steep elevation gradients, heterogeneous 
landscapes, and high spectral variability. This study aims to evaluate the six 
commonly used supervised classification algorithms in Sankhuwasabha District of 
Eastern Nepal using open-source Landsat and Sentinel-2A satellite imagery.

Support Vector Machine (SVM), Parallelepiped (PP), Artificial Neural Network (ANN), 
Random Forest (RF), and Minimum Distance (MD). Sankhuwasabha District in eastern 
Nepal was chosen as the evaluation site due to its complex terrain (elevation range 
247–8485 m) where field visit was conducted in the north–south and east–west 
transect to collect the training and test samples (1100 sample points).

Classification, Support Vector Machine, Parallelepiped, Minimum Distance, Artificial 
Neural Network, and Random Forest, using both Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2A imagery 
for land use land cover mapping in Sankhuwasabha District, a topographically complex 
Himalayan landscape.

Taken together, these results make three main contributions. First, they provide direct, 
controlled evidence that Random Forest is the most reliable classifier for LULC mapping 
in complex Himalayan terrain across two of the most widely used open-access sensors, 
which offers practical guidance for researchers and land managers working in similar 
mountain environments. Second, they demonstrate that the choice of classifier matters 
more than the choice of sensor when working in heterogeneous mountain landscapes, 
which should inform how future studies prioritize their methodological decisions.

using the methods evaluated here can support resource management for soil, vegetation, 
and water, and can help detect land use change over time, including deforestation, urban

sustainable resource management.

1. Introduction
Land Use Land Cover (LULC) refers to the classification of the Earth’s surface based on its physical cover and
how humans utilize the land. Land cover includes natural and artificial features such as vegetation, water, and urban
infrastructure, while land use describes purposes such as agriculture, settlement, or recreation. Remote sensing technologies enable detailed LULC mapping by analyzing satellite imagery to monitor, map, and manage landscapes over
time [1].

3. Materials and Methods
3.1. Materials
This work utilized a range of remote sensing datasets and cloud computing resources to facilitate LULC classification:
• Satellite Imagery:
– Sentinel-2: Level-2A surface reflectance images from the Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, providing 10–
20m spatial resolution across visible, near-infrared, and shortwave-infrared bands.
– Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS): This product combines Landsat 8 OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI surface reflectance data at 30 m resolution, offering improved temporal coverage and spectral consistency.[18]
• Reference Data: ESA WorldCover 2020 land cover map at 10m resolution, clipped to the ROI and resampled
to 30m for compatibility with satellite imagery.

In Phase 1, as presented in Fig 1, the rectangular region of interest (ROI) is defined in Central India using specific

ensure standardized data handling.

3.2.2. Reference Data Sampling
The ESA WorldCover 2020 map is clipped to the region of interest and resampled to a 30 m resolution. Stratified

Abstract
Imaging spectroscopy enables detailed recording of the Earth’s surface and ecosystems’ properties at a global level.

Imaging spectroscopy enables detailed recording of the Earth’s surface and ecosystems’ properties at a global level. Due 
to the specifications of the hyperspectral sensors, it becomes possible to utilize the hyperspectral data in a multitude of 
applications, among which the mapping, monitoring and understanding of land use and land cover (LULC). The Environ­
mental Mapping and Analysis Program (EnMAP) is a German satellite mission that aims to monitor and characterize the 
Earth’s surface on a global scale providing high-quality data with the advantage of open access. This study explores the 
capabilities of the EnMAP satellite in LULC mapping.

Abstract
Satellite Image Classification is a process in remote sensing that aims at classifying 
pixels of satellite imagery into usable information of land use and land cover. This 
information is not only limited to several types of land covers and specific features, 
but it is an essential tool for pattern recognition and storing land information. 
Traditionally, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been popularly used in 
this domain due to their feature-extraction capabilities on grid-like data.

tasks and working with the labelled data. This study compares six CNNs models 
(CNN, InceptionV3, VGG16, Xception, ResNet50, ResNet101) and a Transformer model 
(Google ViT-Base-Patch16-224-in21k) on the UC Merced Land Use dataset. All models 
were trained and evaluated under identical computational conditions using a single 
NVIDIA A100 GPU with fixed hyperparameters and standardized pre-processing of the 
same dataset.

the degradation problem in very deep networks [12]. The degradation problem refers 
to the worse performance seen when making deeper layers due to a vanishing gradi­
ent. Trained on ImageNet with 50 weight layers, ResNet50 introduces residual learn­
ing which allows for shortcut connections that skip over tricky layers, making it more 
efficient. These residual blocks called bottleneck residual blocks shortcut connections.

the underlying mapping. This enables the network to learn identity mappings which 
help preserve the gradient flow. The ResNet50 architecture (Fig. 6) incorporates various 
residual blocks, containing three bottleneck convolutional layers with batch normalisa­

idual blocks, containing three bottleneck convolutional layers with batch normalisa­

formance often suffers in feature spaces that combine multiple data sources with redundant predictors.

2.3.1   |   Preprocessing
To construct the dataset defined in Section 2.2, the raw satel­
lite imagery was preprocessed as follows. For Sentinel-­2 optical 
data, scenes with more than 10% cloud cover were excluded, and 
clouds, shadows, and cirrus were masked using the QA60 qual­
ity band and the Scene Classification Layer. A median composite 
was then generated from the remaining scenes. For Sentinel-­1 
SAR data, images were retrieved as 휎0 values, which are pro­
cessed by GEE with thermal noise removal, radiometric calibra­
tion, and geometric terrain correction using the Shuttle Radar 
Topography Mission (SRTM) 30 m DEM by default.

calibra­
tion, and geometric terrain correction using the Shuttle Radar 
Topography Mission (SRTM) 30 m DEM by default. ASC and 
DSC orbits were processed separately to preserve geometric di­
versity, and additional preprocessing steps were applied to each 
orbit. First, border noise was removed using thresholds on inci­
dence angle and backscatter values. Radiometric terrain correc­
tion was then performed using the ALOS PALSAR DEM (12.5 m 
native resolution, resampled to 10 m) to convert 휎0 to 훾0(nor­
malized to the local incidence angle), compensating for topo­
graphic effects on backscatter.

) to convert 휎0 to 훾0(nor­
malized to the local incidence angle), compensating for topo­
graphic effects on backscatter. Layover and shadow areas were 
subsequently masked based on local incidence angle and slope 
geometry. Speckle noise was then reduced using an adapted 
dual-­window Lee filter (Lee 1980) with 3 × 3 and 7 × 7 kernels, 
using the coefficient of variation to distinguish homogeneous, 
heterogeneous, and point-­target regimes following the thresh­

The mRMR algorithm was applied to reduce redundant infor­
mation among features. The method evaluates each feature's 
relevance to the class labels alongside its similarity to other fea­

The Boruta algorithm was used to perform feature-­importance 
analysis based on the RF classifier. Shadow features were 
generated by shuffling the values of each original feature. Each 
feature was then compared against the maximum importance 
score of the shadow features, and statistical significance was 
assessed.

score of the shadow features, and statistical significance was 
assessed. Based on this comparison, features were classified as 
confirmed, rejected, or tentative (Kursa and Rudnicki 2010).
The RFE algorithm iteratively removed features that contrib­

with the lowest contribution to classification performance was 
identified and eliminated; this process continued until the pre­
defined number of features was reached (Guyon et al. 2002).

These findings should be considered alongside several methodolog­
ical limitations. First, the study relies on a single-­season composite 
(June–September), which does not capture phenological changes 
throughout the year and contributes to the fallowland-­bare land 
confusion discussed above. Incorporating multi-­temporal com­
posites spanning spring green-­up or post-­harvest periods would 
capture phenological signatures and improve discrimination 
among these classes, as reported by Sharma et  al.  (2018) and 
Andrade et  al.  (2021), who found notable accuracy gains over 
single-­season composites.

Andrade et  al.  (2021), who found notable accuracy gains over 
single-­season composites. Second, the 10–20 m spatial resolution 
of Sentinel-­2 produces mixed-­pixel effects in urban–rural tran­
sition zones, where narrower roads contribute to road-­bare-­land 
misclassification. Third, the auxiliary climate data were resam­
pled from a 4 km native resolution (TerraClimate) to 10 m, limit­
ing their spatial discriminative capacity within the 581 km2 study 
area. Fourth, despite multi-­temporal interpretation and parcel-­
geometry checks, the absence of in situ ground-­truth verification 
remains a constraint for spectrally ambiguous classes.

ometry checks, the absence of in situ ground-­truth verification 
remains a constraint for spectrally ambiguous classes. Two further 
limitations concern the statistical evaluation: first, McNemar's test 
assumes independence among test samples, and although a spa­
tial split separated the training and test regions, residual spatial 
autocorrelation within the test set may inflate Type I error rates; 
second, the balanced training and test sets used here (700 and 300 
samples per class) do not reflect the natural class proportions in 
the landscape, so performance may differ under imbalanced real-­
world distributions.
5   |   Conclusion
HSIC-­Lasso + LightGBM achieved the best performance among 
the 15 evaluated configurations, using the most compact feature 
subset (31 features); compact embedded selection thus emerges as 
a competitive alternative to larger wrapper-­based subsets in hetero­
geneous peri-­urban multi-­source LULC workflows.

a competitive alternative to larger wrapper-­based subsets in hetero­
geneous peri-­urban multi-­source LULC workflows. The choice of 
feature selection method appeared to have a stronger influence on 
classification accuracy than the choice of classifier, with F1 rang­
ing up to 0.020 across feature selection methods compared with 
0.0024 across the three HSIC-­Lasso configurations. The three 
HSIC-­Lasso configurations were statistically indistinguishable 
from one another and remained equivalent to the best-­performing 
Boruta variants, while significantly outperforming the mRMR-­
based and ReliefF + RF baselines (Holm-­Bonferroni-­adjusted

monitoring, ecosystem evaluation, and sustainable land management, especially in mountainous areas with

2.1. Research gap and contributions
Based on these identified research gaps, the major contributions of 
this study are presented as follows.

contributions
Based on these identified research gaps, the major contributions of 
this study are presented as follows. 
1) Existing methods rely on fused feature representations, limiting 
explicit modeling of inter-feature spectral relationships (Li et al., 
2024; Rihan et al., 2025).
2) Current LULC frameworks lack mechanisms to ensure temporal 
consistency across multi-temporal datasets (Farda, 2017; Ojwang 
et al., 2024; Nguyen et al., 2020).
3) Transformer-based and deep learning models generally do not 
explicitly model inter-feature spectral relationships at the pixel level, 
reducing their ability to capture meaningful feature interactions 
(Yao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022).
4) Patch-based CNN and transformer methods introduce spatial de­
pendency, which compromises pure spectral learning and reduces 
pixel-level fidelity in heterogenous landscapes (Temenos et al., 2023; 
Yao et al., 2023).
5) Hierarchical learning strategies are underexplored for improving 
class separability in spectrally complex environments (Wa´sniewski 
et al., 2022).
6) Explainable AI techniques are mostly applied post hoc and are not 
used to evaluate the temporal stability of feature importance across 
multiple years (Rihan et al., 2025; Cu´e La Rosa et al., 2026; Temenos 
et al., 2023).

4.2. Feature-aware spectral tokenization
FS-ViT presents a feature-aware spectral tokenization method that 
departs from conventional vector-based spectral learning. Rather than 
combining all features into one embedding, individual spectral bands, 
index, and auxiliary variables are considered as separate tokens, 
allowing an explicit model of inter-feature relationships whilst retaining 
physical interpretability (Yao et al., 2023).

was also confirmed with polygon-level five-fold cross-validation, 
achieving a mean OA equal to 0.9765 and a relatively small standard 
deviation of accuracy values equal to 0.0096 in 2023 (Table 6).

together improve class separability and temporal stability–especially for

7. Conclusion
This study introduces a Feature-Aware Spectral Vision Transformer 
(FS-ViT) to classify multi-temporal land use and land cover (LULC) with 
accuracy and temporal consistency on the mountainous terrain using 
Sentinel-2 imagery in the spectrally complex area. By treating multi­
spectral bands, indices, and elevation as individual tokens and inte­
grating feature-aware reweighting with coarse-to-fine supervision, FS- 
ViT achieved superior spectral discrimination and temporal stability 
compared to conventional classifiers.

with overall accuracies ranging between 96.46% and 98.07% and Kappa 
coefficients of above 0.93, which was supported by cross-validation. The 
multi-temporal change analysis indicated that there was an overall 
forest loss of 6.31 km2, with most of the locations changing to low 
vegetation cover, with a little evidence of vegetation recovery and 
minimal urban development, which showed a gradual transformation of 
the landscape by both degradation and regrowth processes.

spectral similarity to open fields, variability in forest

most metrics, achieving higher test accuracies (above 
93%) and mIoU scores (above 80%). For example, 
U-Net with a ResNet-18 encoder achieved a test accuracy of 94.2% and a test mIoU of 82.1%, whereas 
PSPNet with the same encoder reached 91.7% accuracy and 75.4% mIoU.

accuracy of 94.2% and a test mIoU of 82.1%, whereas

min), indicating an efficient balance of accuracy and 
speed for optical image segmentation (see Table 2).
In Experiment 2 (data fusion of 10 m SAR + optical – simple concat), U-Net again outperformed PSPNet on nearly all metrics.

Limitations and future directions
While effective, the Y-Net architecture is more complex than a standard U-Net and requires careful tuning (learning rates, batch normalization between the 
two streams, etc.). It was found that an improper training setup could cause one encoder stream to dominate 
the other. Balancing contributions from optical and 
SAR branches is an area for further research (perhaps through learnable weights or adaptive fusion 
techniques).
Despite these caveats, the approach employed successfully mapped and detected changes in a challenging environment.

Despite these caveats, the approach employed successfully mapped and detected changes in a challenging environment. The integration of SAR was critical, as many optical images of the study area during 
wet season months were unusable due to clouds. The 
SAR provided year-round monitoring capability, and 
its sensitivity to structure complemented the spectral 
information from optical imagery. While effective, 
this framework has several limitations that must be 
acknowledged:
First, the pseudo-labeling strategy did not use 
confidence filtering due to computational costs.

Conclusions
The proposed Y-Net architecture, by effectively fusing SAR and Optical imagery, achieved high accuracy (95.3% overall accuracy, 88.1% mIoU) for complex LULC mapping within the Cauca River Valley, 
Colombia.

Abstract 
Remote sensing-based land cover classification and change detection are essential for 
ensuring environment, planning cities, and managing resources. Accurately extracting spatial 
and temporal information from high-resolution multi-temporal images remains challenging 
due to feature inconsistency, class imbalance, and limited integration of spatial–temporal 
representations in existing methods.

eature inconsistency, class imbalance, and limited integration of spatial–temporal 
representations in existing methods. Traditional deep learning approaches often fail to capture 
subtle variations, struggle to generalize across complex and heterogeneous landscapes, 
leading to reduced accuracy in change detection. To overcome these constraints, this research 
introduces an advanced deep learning framework, GeoFusion-ChangeNet, for high-resolution 
land cover mapping and automatic change detection. The proposed model integrates 
hierarchical convolutional feature encoder with a residual deep feature backbone to 
effectively capture rich multi-scale spatial features.

effectively capture rich multi-scale spatial features. An attention-based mechanism is 
included to improve feature representation by concentrating on informative regions while 
suppressing irrelevant information. Furthermore, a multi-temporal feature fusion method that 
combines feature concatenation and feature differencing is used to effectively capture 
temporal variations between input images. The proposed system is also deployed through an 
interactive interface to enable real-time visualization of classification and change detection 
results.

The proposed GeoFusion-ChangeNet was trained using a supervised learning strategy

445, and 446 image pairs, respectively. The model was trained for 50 epochs with a batch 
size of 16 using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.003.

and semantic change detection objectives.

among the six land-cover categories. Similarly, the change detection branch employed a 
composite Cross-Entropy Loss and Dice Loss formulation for the 36 semantic change classes 
generated from the interactions between land-cover categories. The training process was

efficiently capture spatial and temporal variations.

Abstract
Land use and land cover (LULC) classification constitutes a critical component for environmental monitoring, urban planning, and
sustainable resource management.

how humans utilize the land. Land cover includes natural and artificial features such as vegetation, water, and urban
infrastructure, while land use describes purposes such as agriculture, settlement, or recreation. Remote sensing technologies enable detailed LULC mapping by analyzing satellite imagery to monitor, map, and manage landscapes over
time [1].

3.1. Materials
This work utilized a range of remote sensing datasets and cloud computing resources to facilitate LULC classification:
• Satellite Imagery:
– Sentinel-2: Level-2A surface reflectance images from the Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, providing 10–
20m spatial resolution across visible, near-infrared, and shortwave-infrared bands.
– Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS): This product combines Landsat 8 OLI and Sentinel-2 MSI surface reflectance data at 30 m resolution, offering improved temporal coverage and spectral consistency.[18]
• Reference Data: ESA WorldCover 2020 land cover map at 10m resolution, clipped to the ROI and resampled
to 30m for compatibility with satellite imagery.
